notes.b: Achievement is the result of a student's ability combined with the effort, attitude and health they bring to learning.
points: Intellectual ability affects how quickly a student learns and the level at which they can perform.
Work ethic, meaning commitment to homework, revision and class participation, has a direct effect on results.
A student who values learning and sets personal goals tends to achieve more than one who sees school as pointless.
Poor health, including illness, lack of sleep and poor nutrition, reduces concentration and attendance.
Choosing subjects that match a student's interests and abilities improves engagement and results.
Part-time work during term time reduces study time and can leave a student tired in class.
Parental attitude: parents who value education and take an interest in schoolwork tend to raise their child's achievement.
Parents' own level of education shapes the expectations they hold for their children and how much help they can give with schoolwork.
Family size: in larger families, parental time and money for each child are often more limited.
Family finances affect access to books, a computer, extra tuition and school trips and activities.
A quiet place to study, books and internet access at home support homework and revision.
Family disruption, such as separation, bereavement or addiction in the home, causes stress that can lower concentration and attendance.
Peer groups can encourage or discourage effort: positive peers support study, while negative peer pressure can lead to truancy and disengagement.
Bullying damages self-confidence and can cause a student to miss school or stop engaging with learning.
Poor school attendance is linked with lower attainment and with early school leaving.
The locality of a school matters: schools in socially disadvantaged areas often face higher rates of early school leaving.
School resources, including teacher quality, class size and access to technology, affect what students can learn.
Teacher expectations shape pupils' attainment; low expectations of a student can limit the goals they set themselves.

keyTerms.definition: A student's capacity to learn, reason and understand, which influences the pace and level of their learning.
A student's commitment to completing homework, revision and class tasks conscientiously.
The value parents place on education and the interest and support they show in their child's schoolwork.
The physical and emotional conditions at home, including study space, resources and family stability, that support or hinder learning.
The influence of a student's friends and classmates on their behaviour, effort and choices.
Absence from school without a valid reason.
Repeated, deliberate behaviour that hurts or intimidates another person, carried out by one student or group against another.
The number of pupils for each teacher in a school or class, which affects how much individual attention each pupil receives.
The social and economic character of the area a school serves, which can affect resources and student outcomes.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which a student's home environment can affect their results at school.
questions.model: Any two, three marks each: a quiet place to study, books and internet access support homework and revision; family finances determine access to resources and extra tuition; parental attitude and interest in schoolwork encourage effort; family disruption such as separation or bereavement causes stress that lowers concentration and attendance.

questions.prompt: Explain how individual, family and school factors each affect how well a student performs at school.
questions.model: Individual: intellectual ability affecting pace and level of learning; work ethic and commitment to homework and revision; attitude and goal setting; health affecting concentration and attendance; subject choice matched to interests and abilities; part-time work reducing study time. Family: parental attitude and interest; parents' own education and expectations; family size limiting time and money per child; finances affecting books, computers and tuition; home study facilities; family disruption causing stress. School: peer groups encouraging or discouraging effort; negative peer pressure and truancy; bullying damaging confidence and attendance; school locality in a socially disadvantaged area and higher early school leaving; class size and pupil-teacher ratio affecting individual attention; quality of resources, technology and teacher expectations.
